### Intro

Hi! I use MuJoCo for robotics simulation.

### My setup

- MuJoCo nightly 4.0.0.dev1013420725 (https://py.mujoco.org/) and 3.17.0 (PyPI), Python bindings. Both print the same
  values.
- Linux x86_64, Python 3.12.
- Default options (no margin, `nativeccd` / `multiccd` at their defaults).

### What's happening? What did you expect?

A thin box (75 x 8.3 x 15 mm) lies across the top edge of a large static box (a slab), tilted and turned a few
degrees off parallel to that edge. The slab's top edge passes through the thin box along most of its length: from
x = 345 mm to 415 mm, it is 0.9-3.6 mm inside the box. `mj_forward` returns **one** contact, at x = 340.8 mm, near
one end of the thin box:

```
mujoco 4.0.0: 1 contact(s)
  dist -4.850 mm  pos x 340.8 mm  normal [0.    0.92  0.392]
slab top edge inside the thin box:
  x 335 mm: -5.75 mm (outside)
  x 345 mm: +3.49 mm (inside)
  x 355 mm: +3.52 mm (inside)
  x 365 mm: +3.54 mm (inside)
  x 375 mm: +3.56 mm (inside)
  x 385 mm: +3.58 mm (inside)
  x 395 mm: +3.61 mm (inside)
  x 405 mm: +3.63 mm (inside)
  x 415 mm: +0.90 mm (inside)
  x 425 mm: -9.08 mm (outside)
separating-axis candidates, least overlap first:
  edge slab x x box z    -4.850 mm  axis [-0.     0.92   0.392]
  edge slab x x box x    -5.027 mm  axis [-0.     0.905  0.426]
  box face y             -5.516 mm  axis [-0.002  0.92   0.392]
  slab face y            -8.431 mm  axis [0. 1. 0.]
  slab face z            -10.551 mm  axis [0. 0. 1.]
  edge slab z x box x    -16.103 mm  axis [-0.026  1.    -0.   ]
winning axis: edge slab x x box z; nearest face axis: box face y (0.13 deg apart, face overlap 0.666 mm deeper)
```

The separating-axis test picks an edge-edge axis (slab x edge x box z edge), which is correct as the axis of least
overlap. That axis is 0.13 deg from the thin box's y face normal, and the face overlap is only 0.666 mm deeper.
Because an edge axis won, the collider emits a single closest-point contact between the two edges. That point sits
at the box's end, so the overlap along the rest of the slab edge gets no contact.

With one support point at one end, a box pressed onto the edge can rotate about that point, and the edge cuts into
it. I expected the contact set to span the overlapping segment of the slab edge, for example two contacts near
x = 341 mm and x = 415 mm with this normal. That is what clipping the slab edge against the thin box's y face would
give. When the winning edge axis is this close to a face normal, the face manifold (with the edge axis normal and
depth) may be the better output.

### Steps for reproduction

1. Load the model below.
2. Set the thin box's free joint to the pose in the script and call `mj_forward`.
3. Compare `data.ncon` and the contact position with the part of the slab edge that lies inside the thin box.

### Minimal model for reproduction

```xml
<mujoco>
  <worldbody>
    <geom name="slab" type="box" size="0.3 0.6 0.00635" pos="0.35 0 -0.00635"/>
    <body name="box"><freejoint/><geom name="box" type="box" size="0.0375 0.0041667 0.0075"/></body>
  </worldbody>
</mujoco>
```

### Code required for reproduction

```python
"""A thin box lying across the top edge of a large box gets a single box-box contact at one end, although the
large box's edge lies inside the thin box along most of its length."""

import mujoco
import numpy as np

XML = """
<mujoco>
  <worldbody>
    <geom name="slab" type="box" size="0.3 0.6 0.00635" pos="0.35 0 -0.00635"/>
    <body name="box"><freejoint/><geom name="box" type="box" size="0.0375 0.0041667 0.0075"/></body>
  </worldbody>
</mujoco>"""
POS = [0.378351959, 0.599323405, 6.33253313e-05]
QUAT = [-0.00729818454, 0.0299928649, -0.200104167, 0.979288255]

m = mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string(XML)
d = mujoco.MjData(m)
d.qpos[:3], d.qpos[3:7] = POS, QUAT
mujoco.mj_forward(m, d)
print(f"mujoco {mujoco.__version__}: {d.ncon} contact(s)")
for c in d.contact[:d.ncon]:
    print(f"  dist {c.dist * 1e3:+.3f} mm  pos x {c.pos[0] * 1e3:.1f} mm  normal {np.round(c.frame[:3], 3)}")

# Depth of the slab's top edge (y = 0.6 m, z = 0) inside the thin box along x: the distance to the nearest box face,
# positive inside.
g = m.geom("box").id
print("slab top edge inside the thin box:")
for x in np.linspace(0.335, 0.425, 10):
    local = d.geom_xmat[g].reshape(3, 3).T @ (np.array([x, 0.6, 0.0]) - d.geom_xpos[g])
    depth = np.min(m.geom_size[g] - np.abs(local))
    print(f"  x {x * 1e3:.0f} mm: {depth * 1e3:+.2f} mm ({'inside' if depth > 0 else 'outside'})")

# Separation of the two boxes along the 15 separating-axis candidates (negative: overlap along that axis).
a, b = m.geom("slab").id, m.geom("box").id
ra, rb = d.geom_xmat[a].reshape(3, 3), d.geom_xmat[b].reshape(3, 3)
ha, hb = m.geom_size[a], m.geom_size[b]
center = d.geom_xpos[b] - d.geom_xpos[a]
axes = [(f"slab face {'xyz'[i]}", ra[:, i]) for i in range(3)] + [(f"box face {'xyz'[i]}", rb[:, i]) for i in range(3)]
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        n = np.cross(ra[:, i], rb[:, j])
        if np.linalg.norm(n) > 1e-6:
            axes.append((f"edge slab {'xyz'[i]} x box {'xyz'[j]}", n / np.linalg.norm(n)))
rows = []
for name, n in axes:
    reach = np.sum(ha * np.abs(ra.T @ n)) + np.sum(hb * np.abs(rb.T @ n))
    rows.append((abs(center @ n) - reach, name, n))
rows.sort(key=lambda r: -r[0])
print("separating-axis candidates, least overlap first:")
for sep, name, n in rows[:6]:
    print(f"  {name:22s} {sep * 1e3:+.3f} mm  axis {np.round(n * np.sign(center @ n), 3)}")
best = rows[0]
face = max((r for r in rows if "face" in r[1]), key=lambda r: r[0])
angle = np.degrees(np.arccos(min(1.0, abs(best[2] @ face[2]))))
print(f"winning axis: {best[1]}; nearest face axis: {face[1]} ({angle:.2f} deg apart, "
      f"face overlap {(best[0] - face[0]) * 1e3:.3f} mm deeper)")
```

### Confirmations

- [x] I searched the [latest documentation](https://mujoco.readthedocs.io/en/latest/overview.html) thoroughly before posting.
- [x] I searched previous [Issues](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco/issues) and [Discussions](https://github.com/google-deepmind/mujoco/discussions), I am certain this has not been raised before.
new_candidates.title: Box-box collider returns one edge-edge contact for a box lying across another box's edge; the rest of the line contact is dropped

## Connect rewrites the Damiao zero

On a real OpenArm 2.0, `lerobot-teleoperate` with `bi_openarm_follower` moved both arms' motor zeros to whatever pose the arm happened to be in at connect. The KER leader was not involved. Its plugin does not send a zero command.

In LeRobot **v0.4.4**, `v0.5.0`, `v0.5.1`, and `v0.6.0`, `OpenArmFollower.connect` does this whenever a calibration file exists:

```python
if self.is_calibrated:
    self.bus.set_zero_position()
```

`DamiaoMotorsBus.set_zero_position` sends `CAN_CMD_SET_ZERO`, which is `0xFE` (`src/lerobot/motors/damiao/tables.py`). That stores the pose at connect time in the motor. The calibration JSON we had was all `homing_offset` 0, and `write_calibration` does not store that JSON in the motor, so the `0xFE` on connect was the write that moved the zeros. Each new `lerobot-teleoperate` did it again.

`calibrate()` also calls `set_zero_position()`, after it has asked for the arm to hang with the gripper closed and the user has confirmed. That path is intentional. The problem is the call on connect, with no prompt, whenever `is_calibrated` is already true.

**Tag v0.6.1 and current main** no longer call `set_zero_position()` from `OpenArmFollower.connect`. Connect calibrates only when the arm is not calibrated, then configures and enables torque. A pull request that only deletes the follower call would be empty against main.

The same call is still in **`OpenArmLeader.connect` on main**:

```python
if self.is_calibrated:
    self.bus.set_zero_position()
```

We did not use the CAN leader. The follower path is what rewrote the motors on the releases above. The leader path is the same pattern, still present.

## Left gripper limit is not mirrored

On the same robot, after the stop-based zero, both gripper limits in `config_openarm_follower.py` are `(-65, 0)`. J2 is mirrored (`left` is `(-90, 9)`, `right` is `(-9, 90)`). The gripper is not.

What we measured, on this one OpenArm 2.0:

- The right finger's free direction is negative, so `(-65, 0)` matches it: −65° open, 0° closed.
- The left finger's 0° is a hard stop. Travel toward negative stalled near −2° at about −7.7 Nm.
- A first encoder sample of about −714° (the gripper's first reads are not usable) commanded that finger into the stop and latched error 12, `COIL_OVERHEAT`, on id `0x08`. The rotor temperature was about 53°C, later about 42°C.
- After `clear_error` on that id only, positive travel was free from +20° through at least +74° at about 0.1 to 0.2 Nm.

`send_action` clips to `joint_limits`. With `side=left`, `__init__` replaces the limits with `LEFT_DEFAULT_JOINTS_LIMITS`, so a CLI override does not stick. An open command of +65° is clipped to 0° and the finger never leaves the stop. The left table has to allow `(0, 65)` before a positive open command can move. This is one robot. It is not a claim that every left gripper opens in the positive direction.

new_candidates.body:
### Description

## Summary

In Isaac Sim 6.1, a free cylinder receives a large tangential impulse on the first physics step after a horizontal teleport, despite resetting its orientation and all six velocity components to zero.

The result depends on whether the cylinder contacted the same floor collider before the teleport. A fresh-process control with the **same target pose and zero velocities** does not receive this rolling impulse. Inserting one actual airborne physics step between the two contacts eliminates the difference.

The headless MRE uses **one dynamic cylinder and one static flat box collider**, with no external assets, joints, drives, controllers or RL framework.

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/14ab0142-0e0f-42c0-b7aa-d4a8e43992b1

## Attached assets: 

[cylinder_force_oblique_mre.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/34357519/cylinder_force_oblique_mre.zip)



## Environment

| Component | Version / configuration |
|---|---|
| Isaac Sim | `6.1.0.0`, Python package installation |
| OmniPhysics extensions | `omni.physx 110.3.2`, `omni.physics.tensors 110.3.2` |
| OS | Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, Linux `5.15.0-161-generic`, x86_64 |
| GPU | NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 |
| NVIDIA driver | `580.178.04` |
| Python | `3.12.15` |
| Simulation | GPU dynamics, Torch tensor backend, `cuda:0`, TGS |
| Physics timestep | `1/60 s` |

Each case runs in a separate process with one active GPU. This cylinder MRE is verified on 6.1; a version regression has not been established.

## Minimal scene

- Cylinder: `UsdGeom.Cylinder`, axis **X**, radius **0.025 m**, length **0.06 m**, mass **1 kg**, automatically computed COM/inertia.
- Floor: one static **10 × 10 × 1 m** box with its top surface at **Z = 0**.
- Cylinder birth pose: center at **Z = radius**, identity orientation, zero linear/angular velocity. No initial floor overlap is authored.
- Static/dynamic friction: **0.5 / 0.5**; restitution: **0**.
- Both colliders use contact offset **0.0005 m** and rest offset **0**.
- Gravity: approximately **(0, 0, −9.81) m/s²**.

## Steps to reproduce

Extract `cylinder_force_oblique_mre.zip` and run the scripts using an Isaac Sim 6.1 Python environment. Physics-only runs need just `mre_cylinder_teleport.py`.

The script performs this sequence:

1. Execute one common initialization step with the cylinder in midair, before making tensor writes.
2. Place the cylinder at **A = (0, 0, 0.025)**, set identity orientation and zero velocities, then advance **one contact physics step**.
3. Teleport it to **B = (0, 1, 0.025)**. Restore identity orientation, zero all six velocity components, and read back/assert that they are zero. **This reset does not advance physics.**
4. Advance one physics step and read the resulting pose, velocity, and contact/friction forces.

The reset uses `RigidBodyView.set_transforms()` followed by `RigidBodyView.set_velocities()`. Both A and B contact the same unchanged floor collider.

Run each case separately. Replace GPU index `7` with an available local device:

```bash
export CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=7

# Prior floor contact, then teleport: reproduces the impulse.
python mre_cylinder_teleport.py --radius .025 --forces --output history

# Same target state, but skip the preceding ground contact.
python mre_cylinder_teleport.py --radius .025 --forces --cold --output cold

# Keep the preceding contact, but insert a real airborne physics step.
python mre_cylinder_teleport.py --radius .025 --forces --separate --output separated
```

Each run writes `trace.json`. Keep `--radius .025`: the script defaults to **0.25 m**.

## Expected behavior

After teleporting to B with the same orientation and zero velocities, the first-step motion should be comparable to the fresh-process control at B, allowing for small numerical differences. The previous contact at A should not introduce a large tangential impulse or rolling motion at B.

## Actual behavior

For the **0.025 m radius** cylinder, the first physical step at B produces:

| Case | Rotation about X | Angular velocity X | Linear velocity Y | Friction force Y |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| GPU: prior contact → teleport | **−6.244942°** | **−6.539661 rad/s** | **−0.081750 m/s** | **−4.905001 N** |
| GPU: cold start at B | 0° | 0 rad/s | 0 m/s | 0 N |
| GPU: prior contact → airborne step → B | 0° | 0 rad/s | 0 m/s | 0 N |

The table reports the specified axes; the cold control has small numerical motion/forces in other axes. For the airborne-step control, **all 25 target snapshots, including poses, velocities, aggregate normal forces, and friction-point data, exactly match the cold control**.

In the failing first step, the measured force components are approximately:

```text
Normal:   (0,  0,         +9.810001) N
Friction: (0, −4.905001,   0       ) N
Gravity:  (0,  0,         −9.810000) N
Net:      (0, −4.905001,  ~0       ) N
```

Normal force and gravity essentially cancel, leaving the large lateral force. The lateral friction reaches approximately `mu × normal_force` despite the zero velocity read back immediately before stepping.

Physics-only and recorded runs produce identical native poses, velocities and contact/friction samples. Net force agrees with `mass × Δvelocity / dt` within **1.3 × 10⁻⁶ N** across both recorded runs.

### Additional controls at a different size

The same script was also tested with **radius 0.25 m / length 0.6 m**, keeping mass at 1 kg:

| Case, radius 0.25 m | First-step rotation about X |
|---|---:|
| GPU, prior contact → teleport, friction 0.5 | −0.624267° |
| GPU, cold start, friction 0.5 | −0.000005931° |
| CPU, prior contact → teleport, friction 0.5 | −0.000006197° |
| GPU, prior contact → teleport, friction 0 | −0.000009887° |

The CPU control disables GPU dynamics and uses MBP broadphase. These CPU/zero-friction results are for the **0.25 m** variant, not the **0.025 m** variant shown in the videos. They can be reproduced with `--radius .25 --cpu` or `--radius .25 --mu 0`, respectively.

## Videos and attachments

`cylinder_force_oblique_mre.zip` contains two scripts, two videos, `README.txt`, and `forces.csv`:

- **`continuous_forces.mp4`** preserves the preceding contact and the next reset. The target reset is shown at **2–4 s**, and the first physical step after it at **4–7 s**.
- **`comparison_forces.mp4`** compares prior contact on the left with cold start on the right. The first target physics step is held at **2–5 s**.
- **`forces.csv`** contains the force components and magnitudes for all **52 sampled states** across the two runs.

`FRAME 0 / RESET` is before stepping; frame numbers count physical steps since reset. Playback is **12× slow motion with held reset/first-step frames**. Motion is not interpolated or amplified.

Arrow colors: **green = normal**, **red = friction**, **blue = gravity**, **orange = their vector sum**. Contact forces are the just-completed step's solver impulses divided by `dt`, following the [RigidContactView API](https://docs.omniverse.nvidia.com/kit/docs/omni_physics/108.0/extensions/runtime/source/omni.physics.tensors/docs/api/python.html#omni.physics.tensors.impl.api.RigidContactView.get_contact_data). Reset frames do not reuse the previous contact-force sample.

Floor colors, the 128-segment display mesh, wires and arrows are **visual only**; collision geometry is unchanged. The overview camera is fixed and the close-up follows the cylinder.

## Question

Could contact/friction state be retained incorrectly after `RigidBodyView.set_transforms()` on the GPU tensor path? The history dependence and the real-contact-break control suggest this possibility, but I have not established the exact internal cause or verified a disable-strong-friction workaround.

Is this a bug in the GPU teleport/reset path, or is an additional documented operation required to invalidate contact/friction state after teleporting? If an extra operation is required, what is the supported way to perform it without advancing an additional physics step or recreating the scene?


### Isaac Sim version

6.1.0

### Operating System (OS)

Ubuntu 22.04

### GPU Name

RTX 4090

### GPU Driver and CUDA versions

580.178.04

### Logs

_No response_

### Additional information

_No response_
new_candidates.title: Unexpected first-step friction impulse after a zero-velocity teleport using the GPU tensor API

### Description

Currently, to copy a QoSProfile, the easiest way I've found is:

    custom_qos = QoSProfile(**qos_profile_system_default.get_c_qos_profile().to_dict())

This is not exactly ergonomic.

Is there any blocker for adding a `QoSProfile(QoSProfile)` constructor? Also, I'd add a `.copy()` method that would return a copy.

### Motivation

Increase ergonomy of working with QoS profiles and decrease the probability that wrong usage will lead to changing the properties of the predefined profiles.
